Series::sinh¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::sinh() const -> Series
Series& Series::sinh_()

What It Does¶

Applies the hyperbolic sine elementwise.

sinh() is the odd hyperbolic companion to Series::cosh. It is defined for all real inputs and preserves the sign of the input:

  • negative inputs stay negative

  • zero stays zero

  • positive inputs stay positive

Unlike ordinary sine, sinh() does not oscillate. Its magnitude grows as the input moves away from zero.

Parameters¶

None.

This is a zero-argument transform on self.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its hyperbolic sine.

Gradient¶

Mathematically, sinh(x) has derivative cosh(x), so the backward multiplier is always at least 1 for real inputs.

On the current verified public surface used here, the reverse-mode example returns zero sensitivities. So the value transform is verified, but this method path should not currently be treated as backward-ready.

In-Place Form¶

sinh_() is the in-place sibling of sinh(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0});

auto& ref = x.sinh_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1.1752012]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Small signed inputs show the odd symmetry clearly.

std::cout << pluss::series::print(
    pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0}).sinh());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.1752, 0.0000, 1.1752]

Example 2. Shape is preserved on matrices too.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({
        {-1.0, -0.5},
        {0.5, 1.0},
    }).sinh());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -1.1752 -0.5211 ⎤
⎣  0.5211  1.1752 ⎦

Example 3. The current reverse-mode path yields zero sensitivities on this surface.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.sinh();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.1752012, 0, 1.1752012]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 4. sinh() is odd, so negating the input negates the output.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}).sinh();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-3.6268604, -1.1752012, 0, 1.1752012, 3.6268604]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • sinh() grows quickly for larger magnitudes; it is not bounded.

  • Do not confuse its odd symmetry with ordinary sine’s periodic behavior.

  • The current verified backward path returns zero sensitivities here.

Summary¶

Use sinh() when you need the odd hyperbolic transform: sign-preserving, non-periodic, and rapidly growing away from zero. The forward values are verified; the current backward route on this public surface is not.
